title: Fixed-Budget Reallocation Changes the Worst-Performing Image in YOLO Detection: Evidence from Six Validation Runs
content: Detectors emit a bounded number of boxes per image, usually one constant: COCO sweeps maxDets = [1, 10, 100], LVIS fixes max_dets = 300. Images differ in count, so a fixed bound is slack on sparse and binding on dense ones. Given a fixed total of boxes, does redistributing them between images help? We show that it is a distributional rather than an overall performance intervention. Our allocation is proportional to each image's annotated object count, so it is an oracle diagnostic, not a deployable policy. On validation it raises worst-image recall by 5.3 to 10.9 points over three seeds and both heads, but the micro-averaged recall difference is approximately 1.5 points (+1.30 to +1.49 across the six seed-by-head runs), equivalence within the prespecified ±1.0-point margin is not established, and mean recall falls 6.2 to 6.8 points. It changes which image is worst rather than lifting every image: after reallocation the uniform-quota worst image is replaced by a different one. The cost is graded: the sparsest 5% lose 24 points and every band changes sign. Once the budget exceeds the label-count cap everywhere the two allocations coincide and the comparison is vacuous.
